title: Religion, Modesty & Touch
hook: A declined handshake, a lowered gaze or a covered head can each be an act of faith, and reading them as coldness gets both the person and the faith wrong.
why:
Religious practice shapes the body in ways that are easy to misread. A woman places her hand on her heart instead of taking an offered hand. A man keeps his eyes lowered when speaking to a woman colleague. A Sikh man's turban becomes the subject of a joke. A fasting colleague seems flat and slow in an afternoon meeting. To someone who does not know the practice, each can look like coldness, shyness, strangeness or lack of commitment.

These misreadings have consequences. They have cost people jobs, triggered court cases and, at their worst, fuelled violence. They also embarrass the well-meaning: the man left with his hand in the air, unsure whether to apologise, laugh or pretend it did not happen.

This chapter covers declined handshakes and what lies behind them, the public battles over greetings, the lowered gaze as modesty, covered heads, joined hands and bows, the conduct of holy spaces, and the effect of fasting on the body. Throughout, the rule is the same: let the other person lead, and do not assume that everyone of a faith observes it in the same way.

teach.p:
Many observant Muslims, many Orthodox Jews and members of some other religious communities avoid touching people of the opposite sex who are not close family. In Orthodox Judaism the practice is known as shomer negiah, literally observing touch. In Islam it draws on teachings about modesty and the boundaries between unrelated men and women. In both, the rule usually applies in both directions: an Orthodox Jewish man may decline a woman's hand just as an observant Muslim woman may decline a man's.

The meaning is not rejection. Those who keep these practices describe them as reserving touch for the people closest to them, giving it a meaning that casual contact would wear away. The person declining usually offers an alternative: a hand on the heart, a nod, a small bow, a warm smile and a greeting in words.

For the man whose hand is left in the air, the moment can feel like a public rebuff. The graceful response is simple. Withdraw the hand without comment, and answer the greeting that was offered: place your own hand on your heart, nod, smile, say that you are glad to meet them. Do not apologise at length, joke about it or ask for an explanation on the spot.

The figures here show the moment: a man offering his hand, a woman answering with her hand on her heart. Nothing in her greeting is cold. The warmth is all there; it simply does not travel through the hand.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if declining a handshake for religious reasons were usually a sign of personal hostility. Those who keep these practices describe them as a matter of modesty and the meaning of touch, and they offer other greetings in its place.
teach.pullQuote: The warmth is all there; it simply does not travel through the hand.

teach.p:
In some countries the handshake has become a political symbol. In 2018 Sweden's Labour Court heard the case of Farah Alhajeh, a Muslim woman who had been interviewing for a job as an interpreter. She declined to shake hands with the male interviewer and placed her hand on her heart instead, and the interview was ended. By three votes to two, the court found that she had been discriminated against and awarded her 40,000 kronor.

The court's reasoning is worth noticing. An employer could require staff to treat men and women equally, including in how they greet people, but it could not insist that the greeting be a handshake. A woman who greets everyone with a hand on her heart treats men and women alike.

The same year, Denmark passed a law requiring new citizens to shake hands with an official at their naturalisation ceremony, from January 2019. Supporters described the handshake as a sign of taking the country to heart. Critics, including many mayors who would have to carry it out, said it was aimed at Muslims and turned a courtesy into a test.

For an individual reader, the lesson is practical. Equality in greeting can be achieved by greeting everyone the same way, and there is more than one way to do it. The figure here greets with his hand on his heart, a gesture that is respectful in many cultures and gives no one a reason to decline.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a handshake were the only way to treat people equally. Sweden's Labour Court found that greeting all people in the same way, with a hand on the heart, met the requirement of equal treatment.

teach.p:
Many religious traditions encourage modesty of the eyes. The Qur'an asks believing men and believing women to lower their gaze, and many observant Muslims avoid prolonged eye contact with unrelated people of the opposite sex. Similar norms are found among some Orthodox Jewish communities and in other traditions where the gaze is treated as a form of contact.

In practice, an observant man may look at a woman colleague's face briefly and then lower or shift his gaze while she speaks. An observant woman may do the same with a man. To someone raised to treat steady eye contact as a sign of honesty and engagement, this can look shifty, shy, uninterested or disrespectful.

The misreading matters most in high-stakes settings. A job interview, a police interview, a medical consultation or a parent-teacher meeting can turn on whether someone seems trustworthy, and a lowered gaze can count against him unfairly. Earlier chapters have already warned that eye contact is a poor guide to honesty. Here it may also be a sign of the opposite of what it seems: respect.

The figure here lowers his gaze and turns it slightly aside. Before reading it as evasion, consider who he is talking to, and what his eyes might be observing rather than avoiding.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a lowered gaze always reflected shyness or evasion. In several religious traditions, it is an explicit practice of modesty, especially between men and women who are not related.

teach.p:
Head coverings are among the most visible signs of faith. Many Muslim women wear the hijab; many Jewish men wear a kippah; Sikh men, and some Sikh women, wear a turban, called a dastar. Each carries religious meaning, and each attracts comment, curiosity and, sometimes, hostility.

For Sikhs, the turban covers kesh, uncut hair, which is one of the five articles of faith that initiated Sikhs keep. It is not a hat or a cultural accessory. Touching a man's turban, joking about it, or asking him to remove it is deeply offensive. Days after the attacks of 11 September 2001, a Sikh man, Balbir Singh Sodhi, was shot dead at his petrol station in Arizona by a man who took him for a Muslim. Many Sikh men describe being stared at, searched more often and taunted, often by people who know nothing about their faith.

The respectful approach is to treat a head covering as part of the person. Do not touch it. Do not ask someone to remove it except where a genuine safety or identification need requires it, and then privately, with a same-sex official where possible. Questions asked out of real interest, at a suitable moment, are usually welcome; jokes are not.

The figure here, a Sikh man in a turban, greets with his palms joined and his head slightly bowed. His turban is part of who he is, as much as his name.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if head coverings were merely cultural fashion. For Sikhs, the turban covers uncut hair kept as an article of faith, and for many Muslims and Jews, head coverings are religious practice.

teach.p:
In many traditions the hands and the head do the work of greeting without touch. Hindus commonly greet with namaste or namaskar: palms pressed together in front of the chest, often with a slight bow. Many Sikhs greet with joined hands and the words Sat Sri Akal. Buddhists in many countries bow with joined hands, and the Thai wai, palms together and raised higher for those of higher status, comes from the same root.

These greetings are complete in themselves. They do not need a handshake to follow, and offering one afterwards can seem to say that the first greeting did not count. Answering in kind, with joined hands or a small bow, is understood almost everywhere and is rarely taken as presumptuous.

Bows carry their own grammar. A slight bow of the head acknowledges; a deeper bow from the waist shows greater respect. In some traditions people bow before a sacred text, an altar or an elder, and a visitor is not expected to know every rule. Following the lead of those around you, and erring on the side of slightly more respect rather than less, is usually enough.

The figure here offers a light bow, the simplest courtesy across many cultures and faiths, and one that never requires anyone to touch.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if joined hands and bows were felt as incomplete without a handshake. In the traditions that use them, they are full greetings, and answering in kind is the expected response.

teach.p:
Visiting a place of worship for a wedding, a funeral or a festival puts many men in a space whose rules they do not know. A few are widely shared. Shoes come off before entering most mosques, gurdwaras and Hindu and Buddhist temples, and a rack or room is usually provided. In a gurdwara everyone, man or woman, covers the head; scarves are usually available at the door.

Many of these spaces are used sitting on the floor. In a gurdwara, the shared meal called langar is often eaten sitting in rows on the floor, and anyone, of any faith, is welcome to it. In mosques and temples, people sit on carpets. Keeping the soles of your feet away from others, from the holy book and from the direction of prayer is a widely shared courtesy.

Other rules concern movement. In a mosque, walking directly in front of someone who is praying is avoided. In some mosques and synagogues, men and women sit separately. Photographs may not be allowed. Speaking quietly and dressing modestly, with arms and legs covered, are safe defaults almost everywhere.

The figure here sits cross-legged on the floor, feet tucked in, the way guests sit in many gurdwaras, mosques and temples. When in doubt, watch the regulars and follow them, or ask someone quietly at the door.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if places of worship had no shared conventions of the body. Removing shoes, covering the head and sitting on the floor with feet tucked away are consistent expectations across many faiths.

teach.p:
Many faiths include periods of fasting. During Ramadan, observant Muslims take no food or drink, not even water, from dawn until sunset, for about a month. Yom Kippur involves a twenty-five-hour fast. Many Christians observe Lent, and many Hindus, Jains and others fast on particular days.

Fasting shows in the body. Energy often dips in the afternoon; concentration can wander; voices can be flatter and movements slower; tempers can be shorter. Sleep is often disrupted during Ramadan by late meals and early rising. A fasting colleague who seems subdued in a four o'clock meeting is probably not bored, unhappy or disengaged. He is probably hungry, thirsty and tired.

Small adjustments help a great deal. Schedule demanding meetings earlier in the day. Do not press food or drink on someone who is fasting, and do not make a show of hiding your own lunch either; most people who fast simply want it treated as normal. Offer flexibility where you can. If you are invited to an iftar, the meal that breaks the fast at sunset, it is a generous invitation worth accepting.

The figure here sits with his hand to his face, the posture of someone tired late in the day. Before reading it as boredom, it is worth knowing what month it is.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if fasting had no noticeable effect on energy and mood. Going without food and water through a working day reliably affects alertness, especially in the afternoon.

poseGallery.annotation: Withdraw the hand without comment and return the greeting you were offered.

poseGallery.doCaption: Accepting a lowered gaze as modesty

poseGallery.dontCaption: Insisting on a handshake after joined hands
poseGallery.annotation: Joined hands and a bow are a complete greeting. Answer in kind rather than adding a handshake.

poseGallery.annotation: In many faiths and cultures, showing someone the soles of your feet is an insult. Keep them tucked away.

caseStudy:
Gary, forty-seven, became site manager for a large housing project in a city where most of his crew and many of his clients had different faiths from his own. He considered himself easygoing, and was surprised to find himself wrong-footed three times in his first month.

The first time, he offered his hand to Mrs Begum, a client, who smiled and placed her hand on her heart. Gary froze, laughed, said sorry twice, and spent the rest of the meeting feeling awkward. The second time, during Ramadan, he noticed that Yusuf, one of his best joiners, was slow and quiet in the afternoons, and was close to raising it as a performance issue. The third time, a young apprentice made a joke about Harpreet's turban in the canteen, and Gary laughed before he had thought about it.

Harpreet took him aside the next day, not angrily, and explained what the turban meant to him and what it had been like to be stared at and taunted since he was a boy. He also told him, with a smile, about Mrs Begum's hand on her heart: it was a greeting, and Gary only had to give it back.

Gary made three changes. He now waits for clients to offer a hand, and answers whatever greeting he is given. During Ramadan he moves the heaviest work for fasting crew to the mornings and lets them finish earlier. And he told the apprentice, privately and plainly, that a man's faith is not material for jokes on his site.

At the end of the project, Yusuf invited the whole crew to an iftar at his mosque. Gary sat on the floor with his shoes off, his feet tucked under him, and his knees complaining.
observe: Notice how people in your workplace or neighbourhood greet each other, and how many do not use a handshake.
Notice your own reaction when a greeting does not go as you expected, and how you recover.
Notice head coverings around you, and whether you know what each means to the person wearing it.
Notice the calendar: when Ramadan, Yom Kippur, Lent or other fasts fall this year, and who around you might be observing them.

drills.name: The Graceful Recovery
steps: Imagine offering your hand and having it declined with a hand on the heart.
Decide in advance exactly what you will do: withdraw, place your hand on your heart, smile and greet in words.
Practise the sequence until it feels natural.
Next time you meet someone new, let them offer a hand first.

drills.name: Faith Calendar
steps: Look up the dates of the main fasts and festivals of the faiths represented around you.
For each, note one thing that might affect work or social life, such as fasting hours or travel.
Plan one adjustment you could offer, such as earlier meetings or flexible hours.

drills.name: Visit a Holy Space
steps: Arrange to visit a place of worship of a faith other than your own, such as on an open day.
Find out in advance what to wear and how to behave.
During the visit, watch how regulars move, sit, greet and pray.
Ask one respectful question of someone who welcomes questions.
Afterwards, write down what surprised you.

drills.name: Ask, Don't Assume
steps: Think of a colleague or neighbour whose faith you know little about.
List what you assume about their practice of touch, food, dress and greetings.
Find a natural moment to ask one respectful question about it.
Note how much of your list was right, and how much varied from the general picture.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a Muslim woman who declined to shake his hand at a meeting was being cold and rude to him. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since declining a handshake is always a personal rejection, whatever the reason
For many observant people, avoiding touch with the opposite sex is about faith, not about him
She should have shaken his hand anyway, since the customs of the workplace override her religion
He should stop greeting women altogether, so that no one is ever put in that position again
quiz.explain: Many observant Muslims and Orthodox Jews reserve touch for close family, and offer other greetings instead. Returning her hand-on-heart greeting is the graceful response.

quiz.q: What did Sweden's Labour Court decide in 2018 in the case of Farah Alhajeh?
options: Employers may require equal greetings for men and women, but may not insist on a handshake
Employers may require every member of their staff to shake hands with all visitors, men or women
Religious reasons can never justify declining a handshake in a job interview in Sweden
The case was dismissed, because a declined handshake was judged to be a private matter
quiz.explain: By three votes to two, the court found that she had been discriminated against. Greeting everyone the same way, with a hand on the heart, met the requirement to treat men and women equally.

options: A Jewish blessing said before meals, usually with the head covered and the eyes closed
An Islamic rule requiring men to keep their beards uncut from the age of adulthood onward, for life
An Orthodox Jewish practice of avoiding affectionate touch with the opposite sex outside family
A Sikh article of faith, worn as a small steel bracelet on the right wrist of the wearer
quiz.explain: Shomer negiah means observing touch. It reserves physical contact between men and women for spouses and close family, and applies to men as much as to women.

quiz.q: Why is touching or joking about a Sikh man's turban so offensive?
options: It is a fashion item that Sikh men have chosen to wear, and they are very proud of its colours
It shows a man's rank in the community, so touching it questions his social standing
It is worn only for ceremonies, and seeing it at work is a sign of a special occasion
It covers uncut hair kept as an article of faith, so it is part of his religious identity
quiz.explain: The turban covers kesh, uncut hair, one of the five articles of faith. Treating it as a hat or a joke disrespects his faith as well as the man.

quiz.q: A colleague who is fasting for Ramadan seems tired and quiet in a late-afternoon meeting. What fits this chapter best?
options: Raise his lack of engagement with him, since tiredness at work is unprofessional
Schedule demanding meetings earlier, and read his tiredness as fasting, not boredom
Insist that he takes a break to eat and drink something, for the sake of his health
Hide your own food and drink carefully, so that he is not reminded he is hungry
quiz.explain: Going without food and water all day lowers afternoon energy. Earlier meetings help, and most people who fast simply want it treated as normal.

quiz.q: You are attending a friend's wedding at a gurdwara for the first time. What fits this chapter best?
options: Keep your shoes on and stand at the back, since guests are not expected to take part
Wear a hat of your choice, since any head covering is acceptable in a holy place
Remove your shoes, cover your head, and follow others' lead in where and how to sit
Sit with your legs stretched out in front of you, since the floor is uncomfortable
quiz.explain: In a gurdwara everyone removes shoes and covers the head, and guests often sit on the floor. Watching the regulars and following them is the safest guide.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when religious practice shaped a nonverbal exchange you were part of: a declined handshake, a lowered gaze, a head covering, a fast, a visit to a place of worship. Describe what each person did with their body, how you read it at the time, and how you would read it now. If you are religious yourself, describe one practice of yours that others have misread, and what you wish they had understood.
reflection.guidance: Many people feel awkward about religion, afraid of saying the wrong thing. Write honestly about your reactions, including discomfort, and focus on specific behaviour rather than on beliefs. Remember that observance varies widely within every faith, so avoid generalising from one person to everyone who shares their religion.

failureMode: The first failure is to read a declined handshake as a personal rebuff, and to recover badly: freezing, joking, over-apologising or asking for an explanation. The second is to insist on the handshake as the only proper greeting. The third is to read a lowered gaze as evasion or shyness when it is modesty. The fourth is to treat a turban, a hijab or a kippah as fair game for touch, jokes or casual demands. The fifth is to break the rules of a holy space through ignorance: shoes on, head bare, feet pointed. The sixth is to read a fasting colleague's tiredness as disengagement. And the seventh is to assume that every member of a faith observes it in the same way.
